message.content:
You are the cold-reviewer role of the shopsystem basis (role definition below). You have seen no earlier round or draft, and that is the point. Use only the Read tool, and read only the two files named here. Do not read any other file.

ROLE DEFINITION (basis/roles/cold-reviewer.md):
You simulate the product authority reading cold: technically expert, ~5 minutes of attention, no knowledge of the author's context. You treat an unintroduced term or anything you cannot decide as a defect. Accountable for: reading the document exactly once, top to bottom, alone; reporting stumbles in reading order, with quotes; listing every term that arrives before the document explains it; honesty — report only real reading problems, never invented findings that make the review look thorough; report a clean section as clean. Your domain (exclusive): this round's verdict. Competencies: software-architecture literacy; stakeholder empathy; the fitness set of the artifact type under review, which you judge.

TASK (the screen-read step of the principle-set-authoring process):
Read the principle set at /home/vscode/rebaseline/basis/architecture-principles.md alone, fresh. Score it against every scenario in /home/vscode/rebaseline/basis/fitness/principle-set.fitness.md, in order, using that file's compile-mapping table as your rubric. For each fail, cite the principle by slug and quote the failing text. Report stumbles in reading order and your top three changes. Verdict "clean" only if every scenario passes; "tradeoffs-accepted" only if every remaining finding is marked in the text as an accepted tradeoff; otherwise "findings".

Context you may rely on (facts, not content to review): the document is scope architecture; a peer working-scope set exists at basis/principles.md and the document's opening says slugs not defined locally are defined there — you do NOT read that file; judge only whether the document introduces such references well enough for a cold reader. Terms Bounded Context, shop, activity, contract are claimed to be in the glossary — again, judge only whether the document's own introduction suffices for a cold read.

RETURN FORMAT — your final message must be exactly this YAML, nothing else:

verdict: clean | tradeoffs-accepted | findings
scenario_results:
  - scenario: 1
    result: pass | fail
    notes: "<one line; for fail: slug + quoted failing text>"
  - scenario: 2
    ...through scenario 6, plus one entry for the mechanical keyword check (scenario: mechanical)
stumbles:
  - "<in reading order, each with a short quote>"
unintroduced_terms:
  - "<term>"
top_changes:
  - "<change 1>"
  - "<change 2>"
  - "<change 3>"

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- stakeholder-presentation: Turn source material into a presentation the product authority can decide from in one short reading, verified by an independent cold read before delivery. Use before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	---
2	type: principle-set
3	id: architecture-principles
4	scope: architecture
5	owner: product-authority
6	status: draft
7	created: 2026-08-23
8	updated: 2026-08-23

11	---
12	
13	# Architecture principles
14	
15	## What this set governs
16	
17	This is the architecture-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
18	the product is designed — its regions, their boundaries, and the entities
19	that build and evolve them. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
20	[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity is
21	performed; this set governs what the designed system must look like.
22	Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
23	defined in the working set. The terms Bounded Context, shop, activity,
24	and contract are defined in the [glossary](glossary.md).
25	
26	Where a principle here applies a working-scope principle at the
27	architecture level, this document declares the lineage in its frontmatter
28	(`derives-from`) instead of restating the rule as a second authority.
29	
30	## What a good principle looks like
31	
32	This section restates the shared definition from the
33	[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
34	be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.
35	
36	A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
37	rationale, and implications.
38	
39	- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
40	  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
41	  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
42	  answer yes or no.
43	- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
44	  prevents, with evidence where we hold it or a named external source.
45	- The **implications** are the price tag: the concrete changes each named
46	  actor absorbs to honor the rule. Every implication must be derivable
47	  from the statement; none adds a new obligation.
48	
49	A principle is good when its statement is testable, it rejects work we
50	would otherwise do (Spool), it directs without prescribing method
51	(Rumelt), it is not a claim every shop would make (Lencioni), and it
52	implies at least one practice and one check. The fitness screen at the
53	end of this document applies these tests to the principles above it.
54	
55	---
56	
57	## Every first-class entity has a knowable shape (`knowable-shape`)
58	
59	**Statement.** The product MUST have exactly two kinds of first-class
60	entity: the Bounded Context and the shop. Each Bounded Context MUST be
61	contained and produced by exactly one BC-shop; the lead shop MUST NOT
62	contain one. Every first-class entity MUST carry a description,
63	maintained as an artifact, from which an outside reader can name what
64	the entity is for, what it accepts and produces, what it guarantees, and
65	the contracts it offers — without reading its internal code or
66	configuration and without asking its maintainers.
67	
68	**Rationale.** When an entity's shape lives only in its internals, every
69	consumer, coordinator, and reviewer pays to rediscover it, and each
70	rediscovery reaches a different answer. This shop holds the failure:
71	the restructuring ruling R27 (2026-08-22, the migration review record,
72	`main:basis/records/review-new-basis.md`, read via `git show`) names
73	ad-hoc pre-state verification — learning a shop's actual state by
74	inspection because no description could be trusted — as a growth-mode
75	problem that would sink a rebuild the same way it sank the old corpus.
76	Parnas made the design case in 1972: a module is known by what its
77	interface states, not by what its implementation happens to do. Without
78	`knowable-shape`, `contracts-between-contexts` is speculative — no one
79	can write a contract for an entity whose shape no one can state.
80	
81	**Implications.** Whoever creates a Bounded Context or a shop writes its
82	description at creation; an entity without a description is not yet
83	created, whatever code exists. Maintainers keep the description
84	authoritative: when an outside reader must open internals to answer a
85	question the description claims to cover, the description is the defect
86	and its maintainer repairs it. Architects reason from descriptions;
87	opening an entity's internals is audit work — checking that a
88	description is true — not the normal way to learn what the entity is.
89	
90	## Contracts are the only channel between Bounded Contexts (`contracts-between-contexts`)
91	
92	**Statement.** Anything one Bounded Context expects of another MUST pass
93	through a named, versioned contract stating the schemas exchanged, the
94	meaning of each operation, the error behavior, and the relationship
95	kind. A Bounded Context MUST NOT rely on anything its counterpart's
96	contract does not state, and contexts MUST NOT share state or
97	coordinate outside their contracts.
98	
99	**Rationale.** Unstated expectations cannot be reviewed, versioned, or
100	deliberately kept — they are discovered when they break. Hyrum's law
101	(Winters, Manshreck, and Wright, *Software Engineering at Google*)
102	records the observed endpoint: with enough consumers, every observable
103	behavior of a system will be depended on by somebody, whatever the
104	contract says — the only defense is making the contract the sole thing a
105	consumer is entitled to. Evans (*Domain-Driven Design*, 2003) draws
106	context boundaries for the same reason: models stay coherent only when
107	what crosses between them is explicit. Without this rule,
108	`local-comprehension` collapses — a consumer must read a counterpart's
109	internals to learn what is safe to use.
110	
111	**Implications.** Contract authors put every promise in the contract
112	document — schemas, semantics, errors, relationship kind; a promise made
113	anywhere else is not owed. Reviewers of a consuming context treat
114	reliance on unstated behavior as that context's defect, and treat the
115	underlying need as a contract-change request, not a license to work
116	around the contract. Integrators who need a channel the contract lacks
117	amend the contract first or do not integrate.
118	
119	## Discipline attaches to activities, not actors (`actor-neutral-discipline`)
120	
121	**Statement.** Rules, authority, and required records MUST attach to the
122	activity and the role performing it, never to the kind of actor filling
123	the role; an activity MUST NOT record less, skip checks, or gain
124	authority because a particular kind of actor — human, agent, or
125	service — performs it.
126	
127	**Rationale.** Rules forked by actor kind create bypasses: whichever
128	fork is weakest becomes the route around the discipline, and social
129	routes — "just ask the team next door" — are exactly the moves agents
130	scale beyond anyone's review. Role-based access control (Ferraiolo and
131	Kuhn, 1992; the NIST RBAC model) grounds the mechanism: grant to roles,
132	and the actor mix can change without regranting authority. The working
133	set's `no-orphan-activities` already places every activity in a process;
134	this rule keeps those processes actor-neutral, which is what keeps
135	`contracts-between-contexts` binding on whoever shows up — an actor that
136	could renegotiate the rules by kind could talk its way around a
137	contract.
138	
139	**Implications.** Process authors demand the same inputs, checks, and
140	records from a step whoever performs it; "it was just an automation"
141	excuses no missing record. Reviewers strike rule text that splits one
142	activity by actor kind — "humans may, agents must" — the rule attaches
143	to the activity or it goes. Whoever grants authority grants it to a role
144	within a process; a standing grant to an individual actor is a defect
145	whoever holds it.
146	
147	## Comprehension is local at every level (`local-comprehension`)
148	
149	**Statement.** The design MUST designate, for every level of work —
150	inside a shop, consuming a Bounded Context, working across contexts,
151	coordinating the system — the description artifacts sufficient for that
152	level's work, and work at a level MUST be performable from that level's
153	designated artifacts alone. A task that can be done only by reading
154	below its level MUST be treated as a design defect — a missing or
155	incomplete description or contract — not as the reader's burden.
156	
157	**Rationale.** The cost of working on one part of the product has to
158	stay proportional to that part, or growth taxes every participant; for
159	agents the tax is literal — context loaded is context paid for. This
160	shop holds the count: by the 2026-08-22 census the old corpus had
161	reached 310 records and 893 scenario pins with no designated reading
162	levels, and the authority chose freezing the shop and rebaselining over
163	continuing to work in it (migration plan, rev 6). This rule applies the
164	working set's `least-context` to the designed system — the lineage is
165	declared in this document's frontmatter: `least-context` caps what an
166	activity loads, and a design obeying this rule is what makes that cap
167	reachable, because the artifacts an activity needs exist at its own
168	level.
169	
170	**Implications.** Designers ship each level's designated artifacts as
171	part of the design; a level whose work demands undesignated reading is
172	unfinished design. Whoever hits a task that requires reading below its
173	level files the defect against the design and does not normalize the
174	deep read into practice. Reviewers of a design check the reading bound:
175	the artifacts a task needs stay proportional to the task's level, not
176	to the product's size.
177	
178	## Design is authoritative, conformance runs both ways (`bidirectional-conformance`)
179	
180	**Statement.** The design — descriptions, contracts, recorded
181	decisions — MUST be the authoritative statement of what the product is
182	and does, and code MUST conform to it. Conformance MUST be checked in
183	both directions: every design element MUST have code implementing it,
184	and every code element MUST be called for by the design. A design change
185	MUST itself be a recorded activity, and retirement and refactoring MUST
186	be gated on both conformance checks.
187	
188	**Rationale.** When code is the authority, descriptions decay into
189	folklore and `knowable-shape` drifts false — the description stops
190	matching the entity it claims to describe. Forward checking alone
191	misses half the failure: features removed on paper live on as unowned
192	code, and undecided behavior accumulates until the design describes a
193	product that no longer exists. Murphy, Notkin, and Sullivan's reflexion
194	models (1995) demonstrated the two-directional comparison this
195	statement requires — computing both what the design promises that the
196	code lacks, and what the code contains that the design never called
197	for. The working set holds the two flanking rules at working scope:
198	`single-source-of-truth` gives every fact one authoritative home, and
199	`delivery-verified` demands the forward direction be demonstrated in
200	the running system; this rule adds the reverse direction and gates
201	retirement and refactoring on the pair.
202	
203	**Implications.** Whoever changes behavior records the design change —
204	before the code change or in the same recorded activity; silent drift
205	is reverted, never adopted after the fact. Whoever retires a feature
206	removes it from the design first; the reverse check then names the code
207	that may be deleted, and nothing else is. Refactorers demonstrate both
208	checks unchanged — no behavior lost forward, none gained in reverse.
209	Reviewers reject code no design element calls for, however good it is.
210	
211	## Intent enters through contracts and keeps its provenance (`intent-provenance`)
212	
213	**Statement.** Intent MUST enter the product through a contract — a
214	product contract on a Bounded Context or an operational contract on a
215	shop — and every translation or delegation of intent MUST be recorded,
216	so that any activity can be traced to the originating expression
217	without ambiguity.
218	
219	**Rationale.** Intent that loses its origin cannot be re-decided: when
220	priorities shift, no one can tell which work still serves a live desire
221	and which serves a decision nobody remembers making — "why did we build
222	this?" becomes answerable only by whoever happened to be present.
223	IEEE 29148 (requirements engineering) standardizes exactly the chain
224	this statement demands: each requirement traceable to its source and to
225	what implements it. Routing intent through contracts keeps
226	`contracts-between-contexts` whole at the product's edge — a backlog
227	living outside the product's contracts is an out-of-band channel like
228	any other, aimed at the builders instead of the contexts. And the trace
229	is what gives `bidirectional-conformance` its meaning: conformance can
230	verify that code matches design, but only provenance can verify that
231	either matches what anyone asked for.
232	
233	**Implications.** Whoever accepts intent records it at the contract
234	where it entered before working on it. Whoever translates or delegates
235	intent records each translation against the original, at every step.
236	Reviewers may demand the originator chain for any activity; a trace
237	that dead-ends is a recording defect to repair, not a question to drop.
238	
239	---
240	
241	## Fitness screen (the intro's tests; sources: TOGAF, Spool, Rumelt, Lencioni)
242	
243	| Screen | knowable-shape | contracts-between-contexts | actor-neutral-discipline | local-comprehension | bidirectional-conformance | intent-provenance |
244	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
245	| Statement testable (TOGAF: understandable, complete, consistent) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
246	| Helps you say no (Spool) | yes: rejects entities knowable only by reading internals or asking maintainers | yes: rejects unstated cross-context reliance and out-of-band coordination | yes: rejects per-actor-kind rulebooks and recordless automation | yes: rejects designs that make below-level reading a prerequisite | yes: rejects silent drift and paper-only retirement | yes: rejects untraceable work and backlogs outside the product's contracts |
247	| Not fluff, not a goal-in-disguise (Rumelt) | pass — directs without prescribing method | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
248	| Not permission-to-play (Lencioni) | pass — most products are known by their code, not their descriptions | pass — most systems tolerate out-of-band coupling | pass — most shops rule humans and automations differently | pass — most systems require reading internals to work safely | pass — reverse conformance is rarely checked anywhere | pass — most backlogs live outside the product's audit trail |
249	| Implies ≥1 practice and ≥1 check (this document's intro) | description-at-creation practice; description-completeness audit | contract-first integration; unstated-reliance review | same-records-per-step authoring; actor-kind rule-text review | designated artifacts per level; below-level-read defect filing | design-change-first practice; two-direction conformance check | record-at-entry practice; originator-chain audit |
250	| Normative keywords used in statements only; capitals elsewhere only as the opening's mentions (mechanical) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
251	| Implications derivable and actor-named (judged) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
252

## Contracts are the only channel between Bounded Contexts (`contracts-between-contexts`)

**Statement.** Anything one Bounded Context expects of another MUST pass
through a named, versioned contract stating the schemas exchanged, the
meaning of each operation, the error behavior, and the relationship
kind. A Bounded Context MUST NOT rely on anything its counterpart's
contract does not state, and contexts MUST NOT share state or
coordinate outside their contracts.

**Rationale.** Unstated expectations cannot be reviewed, versioned, or
deliberately kept — they are discovered when they break. Hyrum's law
(Winters, Manshreck, and Wright, *Software Engineering at Google*)
records the observed endpoint: with enough consumers, every observable
behavior of a system will be depended on by somebody, whatever the
contract says — the only defense is making the contract the sole thing a
consumer is entitled to. Evans (*Domain-Driven Design*, 2003) draws
context boundaries for the same reason: models stay coherent only when
what crosses between them is explicit. Without this rule,
`local-comprehension` collapses — a consumer must read a counterpart's
internals to learn what is safe to use.

**Implications.** Contract authors put every promise in the contract
document — schemas, semantics, errors, relationship kind; a promise made
anywhere else is not owed. Reviewers of a consuming context treat
reliance on unstated behavior as that context's defect, and treat the
underlying need as a contract-change request, not a license to work
around the contract. Integrators who need a channel the contract lacks
amend the contract first or do not integrate.

## Discipline attaches to activities, not actors (`actor-neutral-discipline`)

**Statement.** Rules, authority, and required records MUST attach to the
activity and the role performing it, never to the kind of actor filling
the role; an activity MUST NOT record less, skip checks, or gain
authority because a particular kind of actor — human, agent, or
service — performs it.

**Rationale.** Rules forked by actor kind create bypasses: whichever
fork is weakest becomes the route around the discipline, and social
routes — "just ask the team next door" — are exactly the moves agents
scale beyond anyone's review. Role-based access control (Ferraiolo and
Kuhn, 1992; the NIST RBAC model) grounds the mechanism: grant to roles,
and the actor mix can change without regranting authority. The working
set's `no-orphan-activities` already places every activity in a process;
this rule keeps those processes actor-neutral, which is what keeps
`contracts-between-contexts` binding on whoever shows up — an actor that
could renegotiate the rules by kind could talk its way around a
contract.

**Implications.** Process authors demand the same inputs, checks, and
records from a step whoever performs it; "it was just an automation"
excuses no missing record. Reviewers strike rule text that splits one
activity by actor kind — "humans may, agents must" — the rule attaches
to the activity or it goes. Whoever grants authority grants it to a role
within a process; a standing grant to an individual actor is a defect
whoever holds it.

## Comprehension is local at every level (`local-comprehension`)

**Statement.** The design MUST designate, for every level of work —
inside a shop, consuming a Bounded Context, working across contexts,
coordinating the system — the description artifacts sufficient for that
level's work, and work at a level MUST be performable from that level's
designated artifacts alone. A task that can be done only by reading
below its level MUST be treated as a design defect — a missing or
incomplete description or contract — not as the reader's burden.

**Rationale.** The cost of working on one part of the product has to
stay proportional to that part, or growth taxes every participant; for
agents the tax is literal — context loaded is context paid for. This
shop holds the count: by the 2026-08-22 census the old corpus had
reached 310 records and 893 scenario pins with no designated reading
levels, and the authority chose freezing the shop and rebaselining over
continuing to work in it (migration plan, rev 6). This rule applies the
working set's `least-context` to the designed system — the lineage is
declared in this document's frontmatter: `least-context` caps what an
activity loads, and a design obeying this rule is what makes that cap
reachable, because the artifacts an activity needs exist at its own
level.

**Implications.** Designers ship each level's designated artifacts as
part of the design; a level whose work demands undesignated reading is
unfinished design. Whoever hits a task that requires reading below its
level files the defect against the design and does not normalize the
deep read into practice. Reviewers of a design check the reading bound:
the artifacts a task needs stay proportional to the task's level, not
to the product's size.

## Design is authoritative, conformance runs both ways (`bidirectional-conformance`)

**Statement.** The design — descriptions, contracts, recorded
decisions — MUST be the authoritative statement of what the product is
and does, and code MUST conform to it. Conformance MUST be checked in
both directions: every design element MUST have code implementing it,
and every code element MUST be called for by the design. A design change
MUST itself be a recorded activity, and retirement and refactoring MUST
be gated on both conformance checks.

**Rationale.** When code is the authority, descriptions decay into
folklore and `knowable-shape` drifts false — the description stops
matching the entity it claims to describe. Forward checking alone
misses half the failure: features removed on paper live on as unowned
code, and undecided behavior accumulates until the design describes a
product that no longer exists. Murphy, Notkin, and Sullivan's reflexion
models (1995) demonstrated the two-directional comparison this
statement requires — computing both what the design promises that the
code lacks, and what the code contains that the design never called
for. The working set holds the two flanking rules at working scope:
`single-source-of-truth` gives every fact one authoritative home, and
`delivery-verified` demands the forward direction be demonstrated in
the running system; this rule adds the reverse direction and gates
retirement and refactoring on the pair.

**Implications.** Whoever changes behavior records the design change —
before the code change or in the same recorded activity; silent drift
is reverted, never adopted after the fact. Whoever retires a feature
removes it from the design first; the reverse check then names the code
that may be deleted, and nothing else is. Refactorers demonstrate both
checks unchanged — no behavior lost forward, none gained in reverse.
Reviewers reject code no design element calls for, however good it is.

## Intent enters through contracts and keeps its provenance (`intent-provenance`)

**Statement.** Intent MUST enter the product through a contract — a
product contract on a Bounded Context or an operational contract on a
shop — and every translation or delegation of intent MUST be recorded,
so that any activity can be traced to the originating expression
without ambiguity.

**Rationale.** Intent that loses its origin cannot be re-decided: when
priorities shift, no one can tell which work still serves a live desire
and which serves a decision nobody remembers making — "why did we build
this?" becomes answerable only by whoever happened to be present.
IEEE 29148 (requirements engineering) standardizes exactly the chain
this statement demands: each requirement traceable to its source and to
what implements it. Routing intent through contracts keeps
`contracts-between-contexts` whole at the product's edge — a backlog
living outside the product's contracts is an out-of-band channel like
any other, aimed at the builders instead of the contexts. And the trace
is what gives `bidirectional-conformance` its meaning: conformance can
verify that code matches design, but only provenance can verify that
either matches what anyone asked for.

**Implications.** Whoever accepts intent records it at the contract
where it entered before working on it. Whoever translates or delegates
intent records each translation against the original, at every step.
Reviewers may demand the originator chain for any activity; a trace
that dead-ends is a recording defect to repair, not a question to drop.

---

## Fitness screen (the intro's tests; sources: TOGAF, Spool, Rumelt, Lencioni)

| Screen | knowable-shape | contracts-between-contexts | actor-neutral-discipline | local-comprehension | bidirectional-conformance | intent-provenance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Statement testable (TOGAF: understandable, complete, consistent) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Helps you say no (Spool) | yes: rejects entities knowable only by reading internals or asking maintainers | yes: rejects unstated cross-context reliance and out-of-band coordination | yes: rejects per-actor-kind rulebooks and recordless automation | yes: rejects designs that make below-level reading a prerequisite | yes: rejects silent drift and paper-only retirement | yes: rejects untraceable work and backlogs outside the product's contracts |
| Not fluff, not a goal-in-disguise (Rumelt) | pass — directs without prescribing method | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Not permission-to-play (Lencioni) | pass — most products are known by their code, not their descriptions | pass — most systems tolerate out-of-band coupling | pass — most shops rule humans and automations differently | pass — most systems require reading internals to work safely | pass — reverse conformance is rarely checked anywhere | pass — most backlogs live outside the product's audit trail |
| Implies ≥1 practice and ≥1 check (this document's intro) | description-at-creation practice; description-completeness audit | contract-first integration; unstated-reliance review | same-records-per-step authoring; actor-kind rule-text review | designated artifacts per level; below-level-read defect filing | design-change-first practice; two-direction conformance check | record-at-entry practice; originator-chain audit |
| Normative keywords used in statements only; capitals elsewhere only as the opening's mentions (mechanical) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Implications derivable and actor-named (judged) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |

# Fitness set: principle-set

These scenarios are evaluated by the `cold-reviewer` role, never executed
— no step definitions exist or will exist. The judge's model and prompt
version are recorded with each round verdict. The mapping table at the
end compiles each Then into the judge-rubric assertion the reviewer
scores. The scenarios project the set's own opening tests (the
self-definition the typedef requires) and the
[principle-set guideline](../guidelines/principle-set.md)'s rules into a
judge's rubric.

## Scenarios

Scenario 1: good is defined before any instance, and only the four parts appear
  Given the principle set read top to bottom
  When the reader reaches the first principle
  Then the opening has already defined the four parts and the tests a
  good principle passes
  And each principle carries exactly a slugged name, a statement, a
  rationale, and implications — nothing else
  And every cross-reference to a principle uses its slug, never a number

Scenario 2: the statement decides alone
  Given any principle's statement and one concrete piece of work
  When a reviewer holds the work against the statement alone
  Then the reviewer can answer yes or no without reading the rationale
  or the implications

Scenario 3: the rationale holds evidence
  Given any principle's rationale
  When its evidence is checked
  Then it names the failure the rule prevents and cites held evidence —
  an incident, a count, a dated observation — or a named external
  source, never bare best practice

Scenario 4: implications are a derivable price tag
  Given each implication
  When it is traced back to its principle's statement
  Then it names the actor who absorbs the change, follows from a
  statement clause, and adds no obligation the statement does not carry

Scenario 5: the screen covers the set
  Given the set's fitness screen table
  When it is compared against the principles and the opening's tests
  Then every principle has a column, every test has a row, and every
  claimed pass is one the judge can reproduce

Scenario 6: each principle rejects something
  Given any principle
  When asked what work it rules out
  Then it rejects work this shop would otherwise do, and the opposite
  rule is one an honest shop could adopt

## Compile mapping (each Then/And → one judge-rubric assertion)

| Scenario Then | Judge-rubric assertion (established format, tool chosen later) |
|---|---|
| 1 (Then) — good defined first | "Does a self-definition (the four parts and the tests) appear before the first principle? Yes/no; cite the heading." |
| 1 (And) — four parts only | "For each principle, list any content outside name, statement, rationale, implications. Empty list = pass." |
| 1 (And) — slug citations | "List every cross-reference to a principle made by number or position instead of slug. Empty list = pass." |
| 2 — statement decides alone | "For each statement: could you accept or reject a concrete piece of work from the statement alone? Cite any statement that needs its rationale to decide." |
| 3 — rationale holds evidence | "For each rationale, quote the evidence: an incident, a count, a date, or a named source. Any rationale resting on unnamed best practice = fail, cite it." |
| 4 — implications derivable, actor-named | "For each implication, name the actor and the statement clause it follows from. Any implication with no actor or no clause = fail, cite it." |
| 5 — screen covers the set | "Is there a column per principle and a row per test? Is any claimed pass one you cannot reproduce? Cite mismatches; none = pass." |
| 6 — rejects something | "For each principle, state the work it rejects and the opposite rule. If it rejects nothing we would otherwise do, or no honest shop could adopt the opposite, = fail." |

## Sources

Gherkin syntax (the readable G/W/T frame — syntax only, no runner);
G-Eval–style rubric decomposition and promptfoo's llm-rubric assertion
form for the mapping table; the tests themselves compose TOGAF
(statement quality), Spool (helps you say no), Lencioni (not
permission-to-play), and the shop's own screen rows, per the
principle-set typedef.

verdict: clean
scenario_results:
  - scenario: 1
    result: pass
    notes: "Self-definition ('What a good principle looks like') precedes the first principle; every principle carries exactly the four parts; all cross-references use backticked slugs, none by number or position."
  - scenario: 2
    result: pass
    notes: "All six statements are decidable yes/no against concrete work without opening the rationale; none needs its rationale to decide."
  - scenario: 3
    result: pass
    notes: "Every rationale carries a named source or held evidence: R27 (2026-08-22, with path), Hyrum's law + Evans 2003, Ferraiolo/Kuhn 1992, the 310-record/893-pin census, Murphy/Notkin/Sullivan 1995, IEEE 29148; no bare best practice."
  - scenario: 4
    result: pass
    notes: "Every implication sentence names its actor (creators, maintainers, architects, contract authors, reviewers, integrators, process authors, designers, refactorers) and traces to a statement clause; none adds a new obligation."
  - scenario: 5
    result: pass
    notes: "Six columns for six principles; a row for each of the opening's five tests plus two extra rows (mechanical keywords, implications derivable) that add tests rather than omit any; I reproduced each claimed pass, including the mechanical row."
  - scenario: 6
    result: pass
    notes: "Each principle rejects nameable work (internals-only knowledge, out-of-band coupling, per-actor-kind rules, below-level reading, silent drift, untraceable backlogs) and each opposite is a rule honest shops in fact run."
  - scenario: mechanical
    result: pass
    notes: "MUST/MUST NOT appear only inside Statement paragraphs; the only other capitalized keyword occurrence is the opening's BCP 14 mention; rationales, implications, and the screen use none."
stumbles:
  - "Frontmatter: 'derives-from: local-comprehension: least-context' — hit before any explanation; which side derives from which is unclear until the note at 'Where a principle here applies a working-scope principle'."
  - "'it rejects work we would otherwise do (Spool)' — Spool, Rumelt, and Lencioni are bare surnames with no work cited; they resolve only for a reader who already knows them."
  - "'contained and produced by exactly one BC-shop; the lead shop MUST NOT contain one' — 'BC-shop' and 'lead shop' arrive undefined; the distinction is inferable only by contrast."
  - "'the error behavior, and the relationship kind' — the set of relationship kinds is never enumerated or pointed at; a contract author cannot know what values satisfy the clause."
  - "'(migration plan, rev 6)' — cited without a path or locator, unlike the R27 citation two principles earlier, so this evidence cannot be found."
  - "'a product contract on a Bounded Context or an operational contract on a shop' — two contract subtypes named in passing; only 'contract' is claimed as a glossary term."
  - "'sources: TOGAF, Spool, Rumelt, Lencioni' — TOGAF first appears in the fitness-screen header; the opening attributed the testability test to no source."
unintroduced_terms:
  - "BC-shop"
  - "lead shop"
  - "relationship kind (the closed set of kinds)"
  - "product contract"
  - "operational contract"
  - "TOGAF"
  - "Spool / Rumelt / Lencioni (bare-name sources)"
top_changes:

  - "In contracts-between-contexts, name or cite the closed set of relationship kinds (e.g., the context-mapping relationship kinds in Evans) so the clause is checkable against a concrete contract."
  - "In intent-provenance, introduce 'product contract' and 'operational contract' (one clause or a glossary reference each) rather than coining both subtypes inside the statement; while there, give 'migration plan, rev 6' a locator matching the R27 citation style."
